title: Visiting Medina
hookLine: many visit the Prophet's Mosque, though it isn't part of Hajj

cards: Don't saddle up for a journey, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, except to three mosques.
That's how a report in Sahih al-Bukhari puts it: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Messenger's own mosque in Medina, and the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. The Hajj is over, its rites finished in Mecca.
But some pilgrims, before the pilgrimage or after it, take the road north to the city where he lived, prayed and is buried. Today, visiting Medina.

teach.b: First, what it isn't. Visiting Medina isn't part of Hajj. A pilgrim who goes straight home from Mecca has a complete Hajj.
The visit is its own act, often joined to the trip because the road is already long. Second, the mosque.
In another report in Bukhari, the Prophet says a prayer in this mosque of his is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except the Sacred Mosque.

teach.h: A GARDEN BETWEEN HOUSE AND PULPIT.
teach.b: And he says that between his house and his pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise. Visitors try to pray in that small stretch, the Rawdah, the garden. Third, the greeting.
His grave is there, in what was once Aisha's room. Visitors stand near it and say, as-salamu alayka ya rasul Allah: peace be on you, messenger of God.
In Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet says that no one greets him but that God returns his soul to him so that he returns the greeting. Scholars have discussed how to frame the journey.

Some say the traveler should set out for the mosque, and greet the Prophet once there, holding to the report about three mosques. Others hold the visit to the grave itself to be a recommended act. Both send peace on him.
Fourth, the line under all of it.
Surah Al-Ahzab says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation."

teach.h: PEACE BE ON YOU, MESSENGER OF GOD.
teach.b: Muslims call that sending salawat, and it isn't tied to Medina. It can be said anywhere, in a kitchen, on a bus, inside the daily prayer. The visitors say it a few steps from him; everyone else, from wherever they are.

how: Some pilgrims travel to Medina before or after Hajj to pray in the Prophet's Mosque and greet him at his grave; Muslims send salawat on him in prayer and when his name is mentioned.

o: a journey to Jerusalem's Aqsa Mosque after Hajj
a journey to the Prophet's Mosque, apart from the Hajj
the last required rite of every pilgrim's Hajj

p: worth setting out on a journey for
between his house and his pulpit
ask blessings on him and salute him

s: visiting Medina is a required part of Hajj
a Hajj is complete without it; the visit is its own act.
the Prophet named three mosques worth a journey
the Sacred Mosque, the Aqsa Mosque, and his mosque in Medina.
salawat can only be sent at the Prophet's grave
Surah Al-Ahzab asks believers to send blessings on him, and Muslims say it anywhere.

games.q: you want to set out on a journey for the sake of worship in a mosque. by the report in Bukhari, which mosques are worth saddling up for?
o: the Sacred Mosque, the Aqsa Mosque, and the Prophet's mosque.
games.why: the Prophet named three: the Sacred Mosque, the Messenger's mosque, and the Aqsa Mosque.

practice: If you pray, say slowly, as-salamu alayka ayyuha an-nabiyy, peace be on you, O Prophet, the words from the tashahhud in the prayer, or sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, a few times, unhurried.
If you don't, think of a teacher whose words still reach you, and send them, in your mind, a plain thank you.

wordCard.voice: Visiting Medina. A journey to the Prophet's Mosque and a greeting of peace at his grave, made by some pilgrims, but not part of the Hajj. Today's word.

orig.note: peace be on you, said to one person: the greeting visitors give the Prophet.

carryVoice: Your line: peace on you, messenger. A greeting that can be sent from anywhere. That's today, done.

sources.q: Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation.
